blocks.text: Taste is sensed by special chemoreceptors, the taste buds. There are about 10,000, mostly between bumps called papillae on the tongue, with some in the throat and on the roof of the mouth. A taste bud is bulb-shaped, made of receptor cells with hair-like tips and basal cells that make new receptor cells, and opens into the mouth through a taste pore.

blocks.alt: A tongue with the regions for bitter (back), sour (sides), salty and sweet (tip). An arrow from a boxed papilla leads to an enlarged block of a papilla with taste buds in its walls, and a second arrow leads to an enlarged taste bud: receptor cells with hairs opening at a taste pore, basal cells, axons of sensory neurons leaving at the base, all within the epithelium of the tongue.
blocks.caption: Figure 15.17: Receptors of taste (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 15.17).
blocks.long_description: Labels: Bitter, Sour, Salty, Sweet, Papilla, Taste bud, Hair of Receptor cell, Taste pore, Axons of sensory neurons, Basal cell, Receptor cell, Epithelium of tongue.

blocks.text: When chemicals in food or drink stimulate the receptor cells, they produce impulses in sensory neurons, which travel along cranial nerves VII, IX and X to the brainstem and then to the taste areas of the cerebral cortex. The cortex combines this with other information, such as smell and texture, into the full perception of taste.

Humans have four kinds of taste bud, for salty, sweet, sour and bitter, concentrated in regions of the tongue: sweet at the tip, sour at the sides, bitter at the back and salty over most of the surface, with overlaps.

blocks.title: Try it
blocks.text: Smell affects taste: eat a piece of onion with your nose open, then with your nose plugged, and compare.
